Before the year-end review, one piece of advice, and it is the only one that matters. When somebody asks you how the year went, do not give them a list of months. I have sat through forty of these reviews and the list of months is always the same shape: in January we did this, in February we did that, and by minute four everybody has stopped listening. Give them two sentences instead. The first one is what changed, and it is in the past: we rolled out the new template in March. The second one is what is still true today, and it is not in the past: since then, not one report has been late. That is the whole structure. What happened, and what is still happening because of it. If you can only remember one thing from this recording, remember that the second sentence is the one they will repeat to their own boss.

I was asked last week how long it took us to fix the reporting, and I gave the wrong answer. I said three months, because that is what the calendar says. March to June. But that is not really the answer, and I have thought about it since. It took three months to catch up on the backlog. It has taken a year for the team to stop asking permission before improving something, and honestly that part is not finished. Two people have been promoted, nobody has left, and eleven small steps have disappeared from the process without a single meeting about any of them. If somebody asks me the same question next year, I am going to say the same thing I should have said last week. The catching up took three months. The change is still going on.
